lesson.title: Beyond the Bell Curve: Meet the Chi-Square Distribution
lesson.summary: The chi-square distribution is a family of right-skewed, non-negative distributions, one for each value of degrees of freedom, used to measure how far a set of observed counts falls from what was expected.
lesson.body:
Every distribution studied so far in this course, the normal distribution and the t-distribution included, is symmetric and can, in principle, take negative values. The chi-square distribution breaks both patterns. It is built by summing squared quantities, so it can never dip below 0, and instead of being symmetric it is right-skewed, often sharply so. Chi-square distributions describe how far a set of observed counts tends to wander from a set of expected counts under repeated random sampling, which is exactly the job it will do starting with the chi-square statistic later in this chapter.

Like the t-distribution, chi-square is really a family of distributions rather than a single curve, and degrees of freedom determines which member of the family applies (recall degrees of freedom). With small df, such as 1 or 2, the distribution is sharply peaked near 0 and heavily right-skewed. As df increases, the whole distribution shifts to the right, spreads out, and becomes noticeably more symmetric and bell-shaped, a Central-Limit-Theorem-like effect that emerges from summing more and more independent squared pieces.

Critical values make this shift concrete. For df equals 1, only 5 percent of the distribution lies above 3.841. For df equals 10, it takes a much larger value, 18.307, to cut off that same top 5 percent. The distribution has moved substantially to the right and spread out as df grew from 1 to 10. This is exactly why every chi-square procedure must report its degrees of freedom alongside the statistic itself: the same numeric value of the statistic means something very different depending on which chi-square curve it is being compared against.

One more property worth knowing: the mean of a chi-square distribution is exactly equal to its degrees of freedom. So before consulting any table, you already know roughly where the bulk of the distribution sits, near df, and that this natural benchmark grows as more categories, and therefore more independent pieces of information, are involved.
